title: Abuse and the churches
hookLine: abuse and its cover-up in churches of more than one tradition have caused deep harm; survivors deserve belief and justice

cards: Before anything else: today's lesson is about abuse in churches. If it touches your own story, you can stop here, and nothing is lost. A grown man sits in a church office across from an official.
Slowly, he tells what a trusted leader did to him when he was a boy. The official listens, nods, writes something down, and thanks him for coming. Then nothing happens.
The leader is quietly moved somewhere else, where nobody knows. Today, a wound inside the churches, and what the Bible says to those who caused it.

teach.b: Journalists, courts, survivors and church inquiries have uncovered the abuse of children and vulnerable adults by priests, pastors, youth leaders and volunteers, in Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Protestant and evangelical churches.
This is not one church's story.
Survivors describe a second harm: the cover-up. Leaders who moved abusers to new places. Families pressed to keep quiet for the sake of the church's name.
Children who told and weren't believed. The Bible is not quiet about this.

Jesus sets a child among his disciples and says, in the King James Bible: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea."
In King James English, to offend is to make someone stumble.
The prophet Ezekiel had turned on leaders who feed themselves instead of the flock: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?"
And Jesus warns that hiding doesn't last: "For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest." Forgiveness has sometimes been used as a weapon here, survivors pushed to forgive and stay silent.

But survivors and their advocates insist forgiving is not hiding, and doesn't replace justice. Churches in many countries now have safeguarding rules, apologies, and in some places payments to survivors.
Survivors who speak out say what they need is simpler: to be believed, for the truth to be told, and for it to stop.

how: Churches across traditions have adopted safeguarding policies, background checks for anyone working with children, and named people to whom abuse can be reported, alongside reporting to the police. Some hold services of lament and apology with survivors.

games.q: you're a church leader. a young person tells you a trusted volunteer hurt them. what do you do?
o: move the volunteer quietly to another church.
believe them, protect them, and report it.
ask them to forgive and keep it private.
games.why: survivors ask first to be believed, and safeguarding rules now say report it. moving abusers on was the cover-up.

practice: If this is your story, simply breathe, and know you can talk to someone you trust or a support line whenever you choose.
If it isn't, bring survivors of abuse to mind, in churches and anywhere else, not what happened but them now: getting through a day, being listened to.
If you pray, pray for survivors and for leaders to tell the truth; if not, stay with them in silence a while.

wordCard.voice: Millstone. The weight Jesus says belongs around the neck of anyone who harms a child, a warning answered first by believing survivors.

orig.note: Greek: should cause to stumble, the word the King James Bible renders offend (Matthew 18:6).

carryVoice: Your line: believe them. To be believed, and listened to all the way through. That's day nine hundred seventy-four.
